passage: On the bus to the kasba school, Nirmala played the preacher's talk on one earphone and ignored the chatter. "He says most people are lost," Nirmala told Tenzin. "He has the answer to everything." Tenzin raised an eyebrow. "Everything?" At the momo stall after school, a thought arrived: Tenzin was lost, and so were the two girls at the next table. Nirmala noticed how the thought felt: cold. That night Nirmala searched for the figure the preacher had quoted about villages and found a different number from the district office. Nirmala frowned and saved a note: ask Tenzin's aunt, the teacher. On Saturday Nirmala went to Tenzin's mother's shop as usual.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala listen to the preacher's talk?
qa.a: Nirmala listened on the bus to the kasba school, with one earphone.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel on noticing the thought that Tenzin was lost?
qa.a: Nirmala felt uneasy; the thought felt cold, and it sent Nirmala to check the preacher's figure.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do so that one voice does not take over?
qa.a: Keep checking claims against other sources, ask a trusted teacher such as Tenzin's aunt, and keep friends like Tenzin.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel about being described among the lost?
qa.a: Probably puzzled or dismissed; Tenzin's raised eyebrow and "Everything?" show doubt, though Tenzin was not told directly.

grounding: Nirmala starts to think a preacher has all answers and others are lost, then checks a claim and keeps friends.

passage:
By March, Wanjiru had watched every sermon the online pastor had posted. He had an answer for everything, and she started to feel sorry for everyone who didn't listen.

At lunch in her Nairobi school she caught herself thinking her friend Xin, who didn't go to any church, was simply lost. When Xin talked about her weekend, Wanjiru barely listened.

Then, in Tuesday's sermon, the pastor said that a famous scientist had "admitted on his deathbed that evolution was a lie." Wanjiru repeated it to Xin, proudly.

Xin frowned. "Where's that from? Can we check?"

They checked in the library. The story had been made up decades ago; the scientist's family had denied it.

Wanjiru felt hot with embarrassment. She realised she'd stopped checking anything he said. She'd stopped listening to anyone else.

That evening she didn't open the app. She asked Xin to come to the drama club with her, and she started a list: claims to check.

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru and Xin check the pastor's story?
What was Wanjiru feeling when the story turned out to be made up?
qa.a: Wanjiru felt embarrassed, hot-faced, and shaken to realise she had stopped checking anything the pastor said.

qa.q: What steps did Wanjiru take after that, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Wanjiru took a break from the app, invited Xin to drama club and started a list of claims to check, which keeps her curious and connected to different people.

qa.q: How might Xin have felt when Wanjiru barely listened at lunch?
qa.a: Xin may have felt hurt and pushed aside, as if Wanjiru saw her as less worth listening to.

grounding: It shows a teen who starts to believe one preacher has all the answers and sees others as lost, then stays curious, checks claims and keeps diverse friends.

passage:
In the boys' hostel of the Jaipur school, Mridul had become known as "the preacher's boy." He played the videos loudly at night and told his roommates they were wasting their lives on cricket and films. "You're all lost. He's the only one telling the truth."

Kamal, the senior monitor of their floor, sat on the edge of Mridul's bed one evening. "Can I ask you something? Not to fight."

"Okay."

"When did you last disagree with him about anything?"

Mridul opened his mouth, then shut it. He couldn't remember.

"He said last week that eating after sunset makes you weak," Kamal said. "Did you check that?"

"No."

"Check one thing. Just one. With your biology sir or the library."

Mridul did. The claim wasn't true. He felt foolish, then oddly relieved. On Friday he went back to the cricket nets with his roommates and apologised for calling them lost. He still watched some videos. But now he kept a notebook of what to check.

qa.q: What nickname did Mridul get in the hostel?
qa.a: Mridul was known as "the preacher's boy."

qa.q: What did Mridul feel after the claim turned out to be false?
qa.a: Mridul felt foolish at first and then oddly relieved, as if the single voice had loosened its grip.

qa.q: How did Kamal help Mridul without starting a fight?
qa.a: Kamal asked calm questions, like when Mridul last disagreed with the preacher, and suggested checking just one claim with a teacher or the library.

qa.q: How might Mridul's roommates have felt being called lost?
qa.a: They probably felt judged and annoyed, and may have been relieved when Mridul came back to cricket and apologised.

grounding: It shows a teen who believes a preacher has all the answers and sees others as lost, and who learns to check claims, stay curious and keep diverse friends.
